name: Sorting Algorithms
description: Study of comparison-based and non-comparison sorting: quicksort, mergesort, heapsort, radix sort, and their complexity trade-offs.

observation.question: What does it mean to sort data?
observation.completionEvidence: Can define sorting and list common algorithms

principle.question: Why can't we sort faster than O(n log n)?
principle.completionEvidence: Can explain the comparison-based lower bound

application.question: Which sort for which situation?
application.completionEvidence: Can select sorting algorithm based on constraints

integration.question: How do sorting algorithms relate to divide-and-conquer?
integration.completionEvidence: Can connect sorting to broader algorithmic paradigms

creation.question: Can you invent a sorting algorithm for a novel constraint?
creation.completionEvidence: Can design custom sorting for special cases

isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Mergesort exemplifies the D&C paradigm from algebra
isomorphisms.limitations: Sorting has tighter lower bounds than general D&C problems

content.explanation: Sorting algorithms arrange elements in a specific order. Comparison-based sorts have a theoretical lower bound of O(n log n). Different algorithms optimize for different constraints: time, space, stability, and data distribution.
examples: Mergesort (O(n log n), stable, extra space)
Heapsort (O(n log n), in-place, not stable)
analogies: Like organizing a library: different methods for different collection sizes and constraints

practiceProblems.problemText: Hand-trace quicksort and mergesort on the same 8-element array; count comparisons and swaps for each, then explain why their constant factors differ even though both are O(n log n) on average.
A colleague claims a comparison-based sort that beats O(n log n) in the worst case. Refute or confirm using the decision-tree argument.

misconceptions.statement: Sorting is solved once you know one algorithm
misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Curricula teach one sort and move on
misconceptions.structuralReason: Each sort is a point in a trade-off space (time, space, stability, constant factors); 'solved' thinking cannot answer which sort fits a memory-constrained embedded system versus a nearly-sorted log file.

memorized.evidence: Can name 3+ sorting algorithms and their Big-O

comprehended.evidence: Can explain how each sort works and why it has its complexity

applied.evidence: Can implement any comparison sort from scratch

analyzed.evidence: Can prove the O(n log n) lower bound and compare sort trade-offs

evaluated.evidence: Can evaluate which sort is optimal for a given data distribution

name: Quicksort
description: An efficient, in-place, comparison-based sorting algorithm using divide-and-conquer with a pivot element.

observation.question: What does quicksort do step by step?

principle.question: Why is quicksort efficient on average?
principle.completionEvidence: Can explain average-case analysis and pivot selection

application.question: When does quicksort perform poorly?
application.completionEvidence: Can identify and handle worst-case scenarios

integration.question: How does quicksort relate to other D&C algorithms?
integration.completionEvidence: Can connect to mergesort and general D&C

creation.question: Can you design a pivot strategy for a specific data distribution?

content.explanation: Quicksort selects a pivot element, partitions the array around it (elements less than pivot go left, greater go right), then recursively sorts the sub-arrays. Average case is O(n log n) with good pivot selection; worst case is O(n²) with poor pivots.
nonExamples: Merge sort (uses extra space, always O(n log n))
analogies: Like a tournament: pick a referee (pivot), split teams by who they can beat, then recursively sort each half

practiceProblems.problemText: For a sorted, a reversed, and a random 8-element array, choose pivot strategies (first / middle / median-of-three), predict the recursion depth of each, then verify by hand-tracing.
Explain why quicksort degrades to O(n^2) on adversarial pivot choices and what expectation a random pivot restores; name one real-world input that produces the adversarial case deterministically.

misconceptions.structuralReason: Quicksort's average-case dominance rests on random-ish pivots and cache locality; adversarial or already-sorted inputs with naive pivots degrade it to O(n²). 'Always fastest' hides when mergesort or heapsort is the right call.

comprehended.evidence: Can explain why pivot choice matters and how partitioning works

applied.evidence: Can implement quicksort with different pivot strategies

analyzed.evidence: Can prove average-case complexity and analyze partition balance

evaluated.evidence: Can evaluate pivot strategies for different data distributions

transformed.evidence: Can design a novel partitioning scheme for a constrained environment

name: Mergesort
description: A stable, comparison-based sorting algorithm using divide-and-conquer with guaranteed O(n log n) performance.

observation.question: What does mergesort do step by step?

principle.question: Why is mergesort always O(n log n)?

application.question: When should you prefer mergesort over quicksort?
application.completionEvidence: Can identify stability and worst-case requirements

integration.question: How does mergesort connect to external sorting?
integration.completionEvidence: Can connect to external merge sort for large datasets

creation.question: Can you design a bottom-up mergesort for a linked list?
creation.completionEvidence: Can adapt mergesort to linked list constraints

isomorphisms.mappingDescription: Both are D&C sorts but differ in merge vs partition strategy
isomorphisms.limitations: Mergesort uses extra space; quicksort is in-place

content.explanation: Mergesort recursively divides the array in half until single elements remain, then merges sorted sub-arrays in order. It guarantees O(n log n) time but requires O(n) extra space. It is stable (preserves relative order of equal elements).
nonExamples: Quicksort (not stable, not guaranteed O(n log n))
Heapsort (O(n log n) but not stable)
analogies: Like a tournament bracket: split into halves, sort each half, then merge winners

practiceProblems.problemText: Given the two sorted halves [2,5,9,12] and [1,4,10], perform the merge step on paper, writing the exact comparison sequence.
Argue from the recursion tree why mergesort is O(n log n) in ALL cases while quicksort is not, and state what mergesort pays for that guarantee in space.

misconceptions.statement: Mergesort is wasteful because it copies
misconceptions.structuralReason: The copy is the price of the O(n log n) guarantee and stability; calling it waste confuses average-case speed with worst-case contracts. Merge-sorting linked lists needs no extra space at all.

comprehended.evidence: Can explain the merge step and why it's O(n)

applied.evidence: Can implement mergesort including the merge step

analyzed.evidence: Can prove O(n log n) and analyze space-time trade-offs

evaluated.evidence: Can evaluate when mergesort is optimal vs alternatives

transformed.evidence: Can design an in-place stable sort that improves on mergesort

name: Divide-and-Conquer Sorting
description: Sorting algorithms that decompose the problem into smaller subproblems: quicksort and mergesort.

observation.question: What do quicksort and mergesort have in common?
observation.completionEvidence: Can identify the divide-conquer pattern in both

principle.question: How does splitting the problem reduce total work?
principle.completionEvidence: Can explain the recursive decomposition strategy

application.question: When would you choose mergesort over quicksort?
application.completionEvidence: Can select based on stability, space, and worst-case needs

integration.question: How does this connect to the broader divide-and-conquer paradigm?
integration.completionEvidence: Can map to binary search, Strassen, and other D&C algorithms

creation.question: Can you design a hybrid sort that combines both strategies?
creation.completionEvidence: Can design introsort or Timsort-style hybrid

content.explanation: Divide-and-conquer sorting splits the array into halves, recursively sorts each half, then combines. Quicksort partitions around a pivot; mergesort merges sorted halves.
analogies: Like sorting two halves of a deck then interleaving

practiceProblems.problemText: Take the maximum-subarray-sum problem: state its divide / conquer / combine steps explicitly and derive the recurrence for the running time.
Identify a problem where divide-and-conquer does NOT help asymptotically, and explain exactly which property of the combine step breaks it.

misconceptions.whyItFeelsRight: Every textbook example halves the input
misconceptions.structuralReason: Halving is one instantiation; the pattern is 'divide into independent subproblems, solve, combine' — quicksort's partition is unequal, multiway splits exist, and the combine step's cost, not the split shape, decides the recurrence.

memorized.evidence: Can name both D&C sorts and their recurrence relations

comprehended.evidence: Can trace through the recursive decomposition of both

applied.evidence: Can implement both from scratch with correct base cases

analyzed.evidence: Can compare space/time trade-offs and prove correctness

evaluated.evidence: Can evaluate which D&C strategy fits a given constraint landscape

name: Comparison-Based Sorting Fundamentals
description: The theoretical foundations of comparison-based sorting: lower bounds, decision trees, and information-theoretic limits.

observation.question: What limits how fast we can sort?
observation.completionEvidence: Can state the O(n log n) lower bound

principle.question: Why does comparison-based sorting have a lower bound?
principle.completionEvidence: Can explain via decision tree and information theory

application.question: How do you prove a sorting algorithm is optimal?
application.completionEvidence: Can construct a decision tree proof

integration.question: How does this connect to computational complexity theory?
integration.completionEvidence: Can relate to P vs NP, reductions, and lower bound techniques

creation.question: Can you find a lower bound for a non-sorting problem using the same technique?
creation.completionEvidence: Can apply decision tree lower bounds to selection, merging, etc.

content.explanation: Any comparison-based sorting algorithm must make at least O(n log n) comparisons in the worst case. This follows from the decision tree model: a tree with n! leaves must have depth at least log2(n!).
analogies: Like 20 questions: you need enough questions to distinguish all outcomes

practiceProblems.problemText: Model insertion sort on n=3 distinct keys as a decision tree: draw the tree, count its leaves, and compare the leaf count with 3! and with the ⌈log2 3!⌉ depth bound.

Prove the Ω(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts from the decision-tree leaf count, and state precisely which step of the argument fails for non-comparison sorts (give counting sort as the witness).

misconceptions.statement: A cleverer programmer can beat O(n log n)
misconceptions.structuralReason: The lower bound is information-theoretic, not skill-limited: n! orderings require log2(n!) ≈ n log n comparisons to distinguish. Escaping it means leaving the comparison model (counting/radix sort), not out-clevering it.

memorized.evidence: Can state the O(n log n) lower bound for comparison sorts

comprehended.evidence: Can explain the decision tree argument

applied.evidence: Can construct a decision tree for a small sort and count comparisons

analyzed.evidence: Can prove the lower bound formally using information theory

evaluated.evidence: Can apply the technique to derive lower bounds for other comparison problems
